title: The Year of Savings Sal Khan Gave Himself to Make Maths Videos
dek: In 2009 a hedge fund analyst and his wife agreed he could quit and live on their savings for a year; nine months in, he was eyeing his CV.

story.event: Quitting a hedge fund job to make Khan Academy videos full time on a year of savings
story.summary: In September 2009 Sal Khan, a hedge fund analyst in Silicon Valley whose YouTube maths lessons had drawn tens of thousands of daily viewers, quit his job to run Khan Academy as a not-for-profit, living on savings that he and his wife judged would last about a year. Nine months in, as he considered going back to work, a $10,000 gift and then $100,000 from the philanthropist Ann Doerr arrived, followed in 2010 by $1.5 million from the Gates Foundation and $2 million from Google.
paragraphs: In early 2009 Sal Khan was an analyst at a hedge fund in Silicon Valley, working East Coast market hours and spending much of the rest of his day on something that had begun as maths tutoring for a 12-year-old cousin in New Orleans. By then, he later wrote, tens of thousands of students a day were watching his YouTube lessons, many recorded in a closet at home on a $25 headset, and the practice software he had written kept crashing his $50-a-month web host. He was finding it hard to do his day job properly.

He talked it over with his wife, a doctor in training who worked nights and weekends, and they made a bounded bet. They had about a year's savings, enough, he said, to try this without ruining their chances of buying a house. He set the project up as a not-for-profit, though he had never run one, reasoning that someone would see how much good it could do for the money. In September 2009 he quit. "I informally gave myself a year," he told the Chronicle of Philanthropy. Donations then came in five and ten dollars at a time.

Nine months in, he told the broadcaster Diane Rehm, it had become a little taxing, and he was thinking about updating his CV. Then a cheque for $10,000 arrived from Ann Doerr, a philanthropist married to the venture capitalist John Doerr, who had been using the videos herself. Khan wrote to thank her: if this were a physical school, she would now have a building named after her. Over lunch she asked how he was supporting his family. "I'm not; we're living off of savings," he replied. Soon after they parted, she sent word that $100,000 was on its way.

That summer Bill Gates praised the site on stage at the Aspen Ideas Festival, and the Gates Foundation later gave $1.5 million; Google added $2 million. By October 2010 Khan had an office in Mountain View and his first staff. In February 2012 he told a Stanford audience that the academy was reaching about five million students a month. He did not go back to the hedge fund.

quote.text: I obtained a legal authorisation to preserve as much as was necessary for my support and that of my children; for there is surely nothing more lawful in the world than that a learned man should provide sufficient to support his family.
quote.locator: "Sufism", on leaving his professorship in Baghdad
quote.source_title: The Confessions of Al Ghazzali, tr. Claud Field, Project Gutenberg eBook #58977
quote.connection: Khan's leap had a floor under it: a year of savings, agreed with his wife, so the family's footing was not staked on the videos. Ghazali, telling how he gave up his chair in Baghdad and his fortune, takes care to say he kept enough to support his children, and saw nothing wrong in it.

reflection: Leaving a job to build something is often told as a leap without a net. Khan's was a measured step: a sum of money, a length of time and a conversation with the person who would share the risk. When the money was running low he was ready to go back, and said so. That readiness was not a lack of faith. It was what made the first step possible.

If you are carrying a risk for your family as well as for yourself, they deserve to know where its edges are. A limit you have agreed on together is easier to live with at month nine than one you keep only in your head.
invitation: Some time this week, tell the person closest to you one plain fact about the risk you are carrying: how long you can keep going as things stand, and what you would do then.

sources.title: Grandiose Idea Attracts Donors to Khan Academy
sources.supports: Khan's account: by 2009 the site drew tens of thousands to nearly hundreds of thousands of users a month; he and his wife had enough savings for him to leave the hedge fund and focus on it for a year without ruining their chances of buying a house; 'I informally gave myself a year'; nine months in, a $10,000 cheque arrived from Ann Doerr; his 'building named after you' reply; Doerr had been using the videos; at their meeting she asked how he was supporting himself and that afternoon sent $100,000; Google and the Gates Foundation followed after Gates spoke at the Aspen Ideas Festival.

sources.title: When Sal Khan met Bill Gates
sources.publisher: Fortune (9 October 2012), excerpt from Khan's book The One World Schoolhouse
sources.supports: By early 2009 tens of thousands of students a day were using the site and his software was crashing his $50-a-month web host; he had trouble doing his day job and quit; a one-person operation in a closet; the lunch with Ann Doerr and his reply 'I'm not; we're living off of savings'; her text about $100,000 shortly afterwards; Gates speaking about the academy at Aspen; meeting Gates on 22 August (2010).

sources.title: Salman Khan: "The One World Schoolhouse: Education Reimagined" (transcript)
sources.publisher: The Diane Rehm Show, WAMU (3 October 2012)
sources.supports: Khan was an analyst, not a manager, at a hedge fund; tutoring began with his 12-year-old cousin Nadia; in 2009 traffic and letters outgrew the hobby; he sat down with his wife and set it up as a not-for-profit, never having started one, believing someone would see the social return; they agreed they had about a year's savings; nine months in it became 'a little bit taxing' and he thought about updating his résumé; earlier donations of five and ten dollars; the $10,000 gift from Ann Doerr and her larger donation once she learned he was living off savings; his wife is a physician.

sources.title: Sal Khan, teacher to the world
sources.supports: Videos began as tutoring for his cousin Nadia in New Orleans; Khan worked East Coast hours (5 a.m. to 2 p.m. Pacific) at a hedge fund while his wife worked nights and weekends as a medical resident; he quit in September 2009 and lived on savings for the first eight months; $2 million from Google in autumn 2010; Khan Academy remained non-profit; backers including Gates and John and Ann Doerr.

sources.title: How Khan Academy Is Changing the Rules of Education
sources.supports: Videos recorded in a closet at home on a $25 Logitech headset; his wife a medical student who became a doctor; Khan worked as an analyst at the hedge fund Wohl Capital; in 2009 he formed a non-profit and received a small donation from Ann Doerr; Gates spoke about the site at Aspen; $1.5 million from the Gates Foundation and $2 million from Google; first hires in autumn 2010.

sources.title: Salman Khan: Keep It Simple
sources.publisher: Stanford Graduate School of Business (22 February 2012)
sources.supports: By 2009 Khan had trouble focusing on his day job, then in Palo Alto, so he quit and set up Khan Academy as a not-for-profit; Ann Doerr an early, generous supporter; 'By October 2010 all of these things converged' with an office in Mountain View and a core team; his February 2012 figures of less than $3 million invested and about 5 million unique students a month.

sources.title: "Edu"-preneur
sources.supports: Khan worked from a closet office in his Palo Alto home; he convinced his wife that he should quit his hedge fund job; he chose a non-profit over venture funding; funding began to flow by 2010 from John and Ann Doerr, the Gates Foundation and Google.

cross_checks.claim: Khan quit his hedge fund job in 2009 (September, by one report) to run Khan Academy full time as a not-for-profit.
Khan and his wife agreed he would live on about a year of savings.
About nine months in, a $10,000 gift from Ann Doerr arrived, followed by a larger gift when she learned he was living off savings.
After Gates praised the site at Aspen, the Gates Foundation gave $1.5 million and Google $2 million.
Khan had an office and his first staff by autumn 2010.
By 2012 Khan Academy reached about five million students a month.

research_notes: Hedge fund: Wired and the Mountain View Voice name Wohl Capital; other profiles name Connective Capital Management; the story does not name the fund. Khan's title: the Stanford GSB write-up calls him a hedge fund manager; Khan himself told Diane Rehm he was an analyst, which the story follows. Savings period: the Mountain View Voice says he dug into savings for the first eight months; Khan told the Chronicle of Philanthropy and Diane Rehm that the Doerr cheque came nine months in; the story uses his nine months. Timing of Doerr's first gift: Wired places a small Doerr donation in 2009; Khan's own accounts put the $10,000 cheque nine months after he quit, which would be about mid-2010, consistent with Gates's Aspen remarks 'that summer' (2010); the story follows Khan. The $100,000: Khan's book excerpt (Fortune) says Doerr texted about 20 minutes after lunch that she was sending a cheque; his Chronicle interview says she texted that afternoon that she had wired it; Diane Rehm's interview says only 'a larger donation'; the story says she 'sent word that $100,000 was on its way' and does not say cheque or wire. Audience figures differ by date and source and are not combined: 'tens of thousands' of students a day in early 2009 (book excerpt) versus tens of thousands to nearly hundreds of thousands a month (Chronicle interview); the story uses the book's wording, attributed. Later reach: about 5 million unique students a month (Khan at Stanford, February 2012; Diane Rehm, October 2012 'more than five million'); the Chronicle (2013) says 6 million; CMU (2014) more than 10 million; the story uses Khan's dated February 2012 figure. Gates Foundation $1.5 million (Wired) and Google $2 million (Wired, Mountain View Voice) agree. Khan's wife: 'medical resident' working nights and weekends (Mountain View Voice), 'a med student who's now a doctor' (Wired), 'a physician' (Rehm, 2012); the story says 'a doctor in training'. Khan Academy's own history page (support.khanacademy.org) loads as 403 and is not cited. In the same Stanford talk Khan put total invested capital to date at less than $3 million, which sits awkwardly with the $1.5 million Gates and $2 million Google gifts reported by Wired (perhaps because pledged money had not all been spent); the story does not use the $3 million figure. The Ghazali passage describes his departure from Baghdad in 1096 to pursue a religious life, not a business venture; it is applied by analogy to keeping provision for one's family when leaving a secure post.
